items.title: Multilingual Language Processing Using Paninian Grammar: Challenges and Future Directions
items.abstract: The rapid growth of multilingual digital communication has created an urgent need for efficient Natural Language Processing (NLP) systems capable of handling diverse linguistic structures. While modern NLP approaches are increasingly dominated by data-driven and deep learning techniques, linguistic frameworks continue to play a significant role in enhancing language understanding. Among such frameworks, Paninian Grammar, developed by the ancient Indian grammarian Panini, has emerged as a valuable theoretical foundation for multilingual language processing, particularly in morphologically rich and free word-order languages. Paninian Grammar offers a rule-based, dependency-oriented model that focuses on semantic and syntactic relationships among linguistic elements. Its concepts such as Karaka relations, dependency structures, and grammatical transformations provide an effective mechanism for computational analysis of Indian languages and other morphologically complex languages. Over the past few decades, researchers have utilized Paninian principles in machine translation, parsing, information extraction, and multilingual language technologies. Despite its strengths, the application of Paninian Grammar in multilingual language processing faces several challenges, including linguistic diversity, ambiguity resolution, scalability issues, integration with modern neural architectures, and the scarcity of annotated corpora. This paper examines the role of Paninian Grammar in multilingual language processing, discusses its computational significance, analyzes major challenges, and explores future research directions aimed at integrating traditional linguistic knowledge with contemporary artificial intelligence technologies.

items.title: Multimodal AI refines EAU risk stratification in patients undergoing radiotherapy for prostate cancer
items.abstract: Abstract The European Association of Urology (EAU) risk groups guide treatment decisions in prostate cancer using prostate-specific antigen (PSA), ISUP grade, and clinical stage, but do not incorporate histopathological image information. We evaluated a locked multimodal artificial intelligence (AI) model that integrates routinely available clinical variables (age, PSA, and ISUP grade) with deep-learning features extracted from diagnostic biopsy whole-slide images for predicting outcomes after radiotherapy (RT). The model was originally trained to predict biochemical recurrence (BCR) following radical prostatectomy and was applied without retraining to 353 patients from the population-based STHLM3 trial (ISRCTN84445406) treated with RT. Study endpoints included BCR (Phoenix definition), high-risk BCR (HR-BCR), and prostate cancer-specific mortality (PCSM). Model performance was assessed using Harrell’s C-index and cumulative incidence analyses and compared with EAU risk groups. The continuous AI score showed C-indices of 0.65 (95% CI 0.55–0.74) for BCR, 0.84 (0.72–0.95) for HR-BCR, and 0.81 (0.63–1.00) for PCSM, compared with 0.60, 0.82, and 0.80, respectively, for EAU risk groups. Although paired differences in C-index between AI and EAU were not statistically significant, adding the continuous AI score to EAU classification improved model fit for BCR, HR-BCR, and PCSM. Exploratory AI risk stratification classified 18.9% of EAU intermediate-risk patients as AI high-risk and 28.2% of EAU high-risk patients as AI low-risk. Within the EAU high-risk group, patients classified as AI low-risk ( n = 24) experienced no BCR events during 10 years of follow-up, compared with a 10-year cumulative incidence of 28.7% (95% CI 17.3–41.2%) among AI high-risk patients ( n = 61). These findings suggest that multimodal AI may refine EAU risk stratification by identifying distinct prognostic subgroups within established risk categories, although prospective validation is needed before its potential role in individualized treatment decision-making can be established.

items.abstract: Hind A Alsudays,1 Sultanah Alsudays21Department of Business Administration, College of Business, Majmaah University, Al Majmaah, 11952, Saudi Arabia; 2Department of Business Administration, College of Business, Imam Mohammad Ibn Saud Islamic University (IMSIU), Riyadh, Saudi ArabiaCorrespondence: Sultanah Alsudays, Department of Business Administration, College of Business, Imam Mohammad Ibn Saud Islamic University (IMSIU), Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, Email Smalsudays@imamu.edu.saPurpose: This quantitative study examined the relationships between perceived organizational support (POS), Artificial intelligence self-efficacy (AISE), employees’ artificial intelligence learning anxiety (AILA), and AI job replacement anxiety (AIJRA) in private sector employees; it examined the potential direct effect of POS on both AILA and AIJRA, and the indirect effect via AISE by drawing on social cognitive theory and using structural equation modeling (SEM).Participants and Methods: Convenience and snowball sampling techniques were used to recruit 311 employees from the private sector in the Saudi context. Data were collected using an online survey and analyzed using Mplus to conduct confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) and SEM.Results: In the total sample, POS influences AI learning anxiety only via AI self-efficacy (β = - 0.073; p ≤ 0.01). However, AI job replacement anxiety was influenced only directly by POS (β = − 0.184; p ≤ 0.01). These findings suggest that the relative importance of organizational and individual factors varies based on the type of AI anxiety. Finally, Age has a significant and negative relationship with AIJRA (β = − 0.121, P ≤ 0.05).Conclusion: The Study’s findings underscore the importance of individual factors such as AISE in enhancing the role of POS on AILA. items.title: Open Pedagogy, Student-Created AI Literacy Resources, and Repository-Based Knowledge Sharing
items.abstract: Module Description This module combines open pedagogy, renewable assignments, reflective practice, AI literacy, collaborative learning, student-generated knowledge, peer review, open licensing, and repository-based dissemination, based on the Repositories of AI Literacy Resources (RAILR) concept. The module is primarily designed for undergraduate students, although it can be adapted for other educational levels depending on the instructor's teaching goals. It can be delivered as a standalone module, an elective, or with its learning activities incorporated into an existing course. The central purpose of the module is to move students beyond being consumers of AI literacy guidance resources to becoming creators. Through reflection on their own experiences of using generative AI tools, discussion with peers, collaborative resource development, peer review, and open dissemination, students can develop AI literacy resources that can benefit other learners. Instructors are not required to treat every activity as compulsory, except when implementing the module as a full course or an elective. Instead, instructors can select and adapt the activities according to their course objectives, teaching goals, available teaching time, student numbers, and preferred or feasible mode of delivery. Learning Outcomes By the end of this module, students should be able to: Explain the concept of open pedagogy and distinguish it from traditional approaches to teaching and learning. Explain the relationship between open pedagogy and renewable assignments. Differentiate between disposable and renewable assignments. Explain AI literacy Describe the importance of AI literacy for the responsible use of generative AI tools. Critically reflect on their own experiences using generative AI tools. Learn from the experiences of other students through collaborative activities. Transform personal and shared experiences into AI literacy resources. Collaboratively develop AI literacy resources suitable for open dissemination. Develop AI literacy resources for dissemination through Repositories of AI Literacy Resources (RAILR). Target Audience Level: Undergraduate Adaptable for other levels depending on instructors' teaching goals. Suitable as a standalone module or as an elective Module Outline This module is organised into the following sections: Section 1: Purpose of This Module Section 2: Open Pedagogy: From Disposable Assignments to Shared Knowledge Section 3: Learning from Experience: Why Students' Experiences with Generative AI Tools Matter Section 4: From Reflection to Resource Creation: Transforming Experience into AI Literacy Resources Section 5: Repository-Based Knowledge Sharing: Preserving and Disseminating Student-Created AI Literacy Resources in RAILR Section 6: Reflecting on Your AI Journey: Learning Through Personal Experience Section 7: Practical Learning Activities Practical Activity 1: My AI Journey Practical Activity 2: Learning from Others Practical Activity 3: Co-Creating an AI Literacy Resource Practical Activity 4: Peer Review, Improvement, and Dissemination Practical Activity 5: Complete the Appropriate RAILR Dissemination Agreement Practical Activity 6: Open Dissemination of AI Literacy Resources Section 8. Learning and Reading Resources Assessment Students will complete a series of reflective, collaborative, and resource-development activities. Depending on the instructor's implementation of the module, assessment may include: An individual reflective essay. Participation in collaborative group discussions. Development of a group AI literacy resource. Peer review of another group's AI literacy resource. Preparation of resources for dissemination through RAILR

items.title: PCHMR: Empowering and Benchmarking Human Mesh Recovery in Privacy-Constrained Real-World Settings
items.abstract: Fine-tuning directly on user-side data is an effective way to improve the performance of widely adopted data-driven human mesh recovery (HMR) models. However, doing so for existing HMR methods often assumes aggregating user-side data from real-world HMR-deployed devices to a central training server, posing a significant privacy risk as sensitive human images are transmitted. How can human mesh recovery be evaluated and improved in privacy-constrained real-world settings? We study this question through a benchmark in which state-of-the-art HMR models are trained with federated learning and a secure-aggregation variant, neither of which centralizes raw images, and evaluated across a wide range of client-scale and data-heterogeneity settings. We document that common HMR training pipelines are built around centralized data access and quantify how representative HMR backbones behave when that assumption is removed. Furthermore, to study the data bottleneck of privacy-constrained HMR training, we propose DePoser, a local annotation and fine-tuning pipeline enhanced with depth foundation models, with which collaboratively trained HMR models can be locally tailored to the end user's distribution. On in-the-wild data, fine-tuning on DePoser annotations improves personalization accuracy, measured against DePoser-generated pseudo-ground truth. This benchmark aims to support future work on privacy-constrained HMR models and their real-world deployment and evaluation.
